validated_results.title: Associations of energy, fat, calcium, and vitamin D with prostate cancer risk.
validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Population-based case-control study of incident prostate cancer that assessed dietary fat intake, including total polyunsaturated fatty acids, in relation to prostate cancer risk.

extraction.timing: retrospective dietary assessment covering the 3-5 years before diagnosis or interview
extraction.population: Men aged 40-64 with incident prostate cancer from the Seattle-Puget Sound SEER registry and population controls

sample_size.excerpt: This population-based, case-control study in King County,Washington examined associations of energy, fat, vitamin D, and calcium with risk of prostate cancer in 605 incident cases (ages 40-64 years) identified from the Seattle-Puget Sound Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results registry and 592 controls recruited from the same underlying population using random-digit telephone sampling.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 605 + 592 = 1197

cases.excerpt: This population-based, case-control study in King County,Washington examined associations of energy, fat, vitamin D, and calcium with risk of prostate cancer in 605 incident cases (ages 40-64 years) identified from the Seattle-Puget Sound Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results registry and 592 controls recruited from the same underlying population using random-digit telephone sampling.

comparison.excerpt: There were no associations of vitamin D, total polyunsaturated fatty acids, or the highly unsaturated, long-chain eicosapentainoic and docosahexaenoic fatty acids with prostate cancer risk.

design.excerpt: This population-based, case-control study in King County,Washington

timing.excerpt: Self-administered food frequency questionnaires were used to assess diet over the 3-5-year period before diagnosis or interview date.
